narrative:
The model estimated a 78% probability that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt, a high-risk estimate that led to your law school application being denied. This does not mean success is impossible, but it means your application was screened as too risky under the school’s current process.

The strongest reason was your third-year class standing: you were in the first decile (1.00), while accepted students averaged around the sixth decile (5.79). In this applicant pool, that standing was treated as strongly consistent with bar failure. Your LSAT score of 26 also pushed toward failure; accepted students averaged 37.18, so your score was far below that benchmark. Only your undergraduate GPA of 3.10 leaned toward passing, even though it was slightly below the accepted average of 3.23. That positive signal was not enough to offset the two stronger risk indicators.

To improve a future application, focus on what you can still change. Retake the LSAT after structured preparation, seek academic advising and bar-exam readiness support, and consider whether additional coursework or a delayed application would strengthen your record. Ask admissions for feedback and, if relevant, explain any circumstances in a concise addendum. A revised application should show concrete improvement, especially in LSAT performance and evidence of bar-exam readiness.
